results.title: How do you fine-tune an LLM using LoRA or parameter-efficient tuning? | by NS Academy | Medium
results.content: # **How do you fine-tune an LLM using LoRA or parameter-efficient tuning?**. ## 🔹 Why LoRA / Parameter-Efficient Tuning? Fine-tuning a large language model (LLM) usually means updating **all parameters** (billions of them). That’s **slow, memory-heavy, and expensive**. **Parameter-efficient tuning** **(PEFT)** methods (like **LoRA**) solve this by:. * Freezing most of the LLM’s weights. * Adding a small number of trainable parameters (adapters). * Training only those adapters → faster, cheaper, less GPU memory. ## 🔹 LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) Explained. LoRA modifies **linear layers** inside the transformer. 1. Normally, a linear layer is:. 2. y=Wxy = Wxy=Wx. 3. where W∈Rd×kW \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times k}W∈Rd×k. 4. Instead of updating **all of W**, LoRA freezes it and **adds a low-rank decomposition**:. 5. W′=W+BAW’ = W + BAW′=W+BA. * A∈Rr×kA \in \mathbb{R}^{r \times k}A∈Rr×k. * B∈Rd×rB \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times r}B∈Rd×r. where r≪d,kr \ll d, kr≪d,k (small rank, e.g., 8, 16). * Only AAA and BBB are trained. 👉 This reduces trainable parameters drastically (e.g., **<1%** of the full model). ## 🔹 Steps to Fine-Tune an LLM with LoRA. Example: LLaMA, GPT-J, Falcon, etc. 2. **Wrap the model with LoRA adapters**. Using libraries like PEFT (Hugging Face) or `loralib`:. from peft import LoraConfig, get\_peft\_model. target\_modules=[“q\_proj”,”v\_proj”], # which layers to adapt. model = get\_peft\_model(base\_model, config). The library handles this automatically — only LoRA weights update. * **Train on task-specific data**. * Small dataset (e.g., Q&A, summarization). * Use standard training loop (cross-entropy loss). model.save\_pretrained(“lora\_finetuned\_model”). 1. **Merge or load for inference**. * Load base LLM + LoRA adapters at inference. * Or merge LoRA into full weights if needed. ## 🔹 Other Parameter-Efficient Tuning Methods. * **Adapters**: Insert small MLP “adapter” layers between transformer blocks. * **Prefix Tuning**: Learn a set of “soft prompts” prepended to input tokens. * **Prompt Tuning / P-Tuning v2**: Optimize only **embeddings** for prompts. * **BitFit**: Fine-tune only bias terms in the model. ## 🔹 Example Use Case. Suppose you want to fine-tune **LLaMA-7B** for **legal text summarization**:. * Full fine-tuning: ~14B **parameters** → 200+ GB GPU memory. * LoRA fine-tuning: ~50M trainable parameters → fits on a single GPU (A100). * Training cost drops by **10–100x**, with similar performance.

results.title: Fine-Tuning LLMs: RLHF, LoRA, and Instruction Tuning - Synthesis AI
results.content: * then we discuss fine-tuning pretrained LLMs on small datasets by learning adapters for the mostly frozen weights of the base models; the most popular and efficient tool here have been low-rank adapters (LoRA);. Their approach, illustrated in the figure below, is very similar: they collect human feedback on which document summaries are better, train a reward model to match these preferences, and then use the reward model to fine-tune with reinforcement learning. Overall, low-rank adaptation is one of the most popular ways to fine-tune existing large models: even a very small dataset may be enough to train a low-rank adapter, and the resulting model can still use all of the power of the large number of pretrained weights. ## Instruction Tuning and Where to Get the Data for It. For large language models, both RLHF and low-rank adaptation usually aim to bridge the gap between pretext tasks, i.e., tasks that the LLM pretrains on, and actual use cases that involve fulfilling user requests in the form of natural language prompts. With this approach, one can adapt already existing NLP datasets for various tasks, providing one or a few descriptions for every task and thus turning a dataset previously designed to train NLP models from scratch into a prompt-response dataset suitable for fine-tuning LLMs. P3 combined at least a couple dozen different datasets, and later another couple dozen were added by Muenninghof et al. They took the LLaMA 7B model (Touvron et al., 2023), which is a small LLM by modern standards, used a much larger LLM *text-davinci-003* (that’s GPT 3.5, the cutting edge model at that time) to generate instruction following examples, and fine-tuned LLaMA 7B on them (illustration by Taori et al., 2023):. * Rejection Fine-Tuning (RFT; Yuan et al., 2023) takes this idea one step further, developing a better filter for reasoning paths (they specialize in mathematical reasoning, so reasoning paths are chains of equations in this case) based on rejection sampling, looking for the most diverse paths to improve reasoning; moreover, they find a log-linear dependence between the amount of data and model performance and show how better data (e.g., filtered with RFT) can lead to better models;.

results.title: Fine-Tuning vs Prompt-Tuning vs Adapter Tuning: A Strategic Decision Guide | by Amit Kharche | Medium
results.content: # Fine-Tuning vs Prompt-Tuning vs Adapter Tuning: A Strategic Decision Guide. * **Fine-tuning** — Full customization by retraining model weights. * **Prompt-tuning** — Lightweight control via optimized instructions or embeddings. * **Adapter-tuning** — Efficient modular updates through small parameter additions. * **ROI & TCO** — Training an LLM from scratch can exceed $10M; parameter-efficient tuning can deliver results for under $100K. * **Time-to-Market** — Prompt-tuning can launch a pilot in weeks; fine-tuning may take months. * **Talent Requirements** — Fine-tuning requires ML engineers; prompt/adapters can be managed by data scientists with Python. Fine-Tuning: Full Customization at High Cost. Fine-tuning retrains all (or most) model parameters on task/domain data. * **Governance burden** — Each use case = new fine-tuned model to track. ### Technical Example (PEFT Soft Prompt Tuning). Adapter-Tuning: Modular and Scalable. Adapter-tuning freezes most model parameters but adds small trainable modules (e.g., LoRA layers) into transformer blocks. * **QLoRA** — Quantized low-rank adapters enabling 65B fine-tuning on a single GPU. * **P-Tuning v2** — Scales soft prompts beyond toy examples. * **Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT)** frameworks from Hugging Face and NeMo. These techniques are closing the gap between fine-tuning accuracy and adapter/prompt efficiency. * **Model Drift** — Markets, compliance rules, and customer expectations evolve. * **AWS SageMaker** — Distributed fine-tuning and monitoring at scale. * **Databricks MosaicML** — Cost-optimized fine-tuning pipelines. * **Retail Pilot Failure:** A prompt-tuned chatbot misunderstood SKU codes, leading to poor customer feedback → solution: adapter-tuning with structured catalog embeddings. * **Banking Risk:** Fine-tuned compliance bot drifted after regulation change → solution: modular adapters for specific jurisdictions. * **Healthcare Startup:** Launched with prompt-tuning only; hallucinations led to clinical risk → solution: hybrid approach (prompt + adapter). * **Revenue Growth** — Fine-tuned personalization boosts conversions. * **Risk Reduction** — Governance-focused tuning prevents regulatory fines. * **Scalability** — Modular adapters enable enterprise-wide rollout. Fine-tuning, prompt-tuning, and adapter-tuning are **not interchangeable choices.** They are strategic levers with direct impact on **costs, scalability, and business risk.**. * **Prompt-tuning** = speed and cost-efficiency, but limited. * **Adapter-tuning** = balance and scalability. Executives and AI leaders must align tuning strategies with enterprise KPIs, regulatory environments, and budget constraints.
